Up until that point, when I was training like a powerlifter, I was streaming the deadlift exactly like I was the squat. The bench press would be multiple repetitions per set, and I thought to myself, there's really got to be a better way. Because what's unique to the deadlift is we don't get to lower the barbell before we lift it; therefore, we don't get to take advantage of the stored elastic energy, which ultimately becomes what is known as the stretch reflex in the bottom portion of the lift. In the squat, you descend with the bar on your back, you're building tension, stored elastic energy into the muscle cells and muscle spindles, and then you can reproduce force as you're coming on the concentric phase out of the descent and into the ascent. The same is true when you're building tension in a bench press; you're lowering the bar down, you're building tension, you're storing elastic energy within your muscles, and then you produce force upwards.

In the deadlift, you don't have that opportunity; you just have to essentially set up, bend over, and pick up the barbell from a dead stop. So, I stumbled across a training article written by Louis Simmons in the early 90s in Powerlifting USA. And basically, he was talking about Russian sports scientists who had done some testing, and they discovered that, with a stretch reflex, the stretch reflex dissipates after four full seconds. So, if you take a break between repetitions for a minimum of four full seconds, the stretch reflex is gone; there's no longer any stored elastic energy inside your muscle cells, and therefore, you're essentially starting from a dead stop again. So, imagine doing a pause squat, putting the bar on your back, and sitting in the hole for four full seconds. It's not a forward count; that's four full seconds. Anything beyond four full seconds, and you're essentially squatting from a dead stop. So, I posit the question to you: imagine if we competed in powerlifting, and in the squat, we set the bar on safety pins at a below-parallel position, and you had to crawl underneath the bar and stand up. Likewise, in the bench press, imagine if we started with the bar on our chest and then just had to press the weight up.  What do you think about treating the squat and the bench press differently? Well, that's why I choose to train the deadlift differently; it's because the science tells me so. It just makes more sense. Six other reasons: specificity, again... The first thing, you're only required to do one rep in competition, and you never lower the bar before you pick it up.
